title: Q&A: What is the Brazil-led ‘deforestation roadmap’? - Carbon Brief
gist: Brazil's COP30 presidency published a voluntary deforestation roadmap that adds no new commitments but offers a menu of 18 national policies and 10 finance proposals, with a $300bn/year funding need and under one-third currently met. Carbon Brief explains why India and Russia hesitated and what barriers countries report.

insights.claim: Brazil's COP30 presidency released a voluntary 'roadmap' on halting and reversing deforestation on 3 November; it makes no new commitments and does not seek to reopen agreed decisions.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A non-binding process adds no new obligations, so expect implementation-by-country rather than a market-moving mandate.
insights.quote: Unlike these previous pledges, the roadmap does not make any new commitments.

insights.claim: The roadmap fell outside COP30's negotiated outcomes because about 100 countries supported it, short of the 196 parties required for consensus; the presidency instead pursued it outside the COP process.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Illustrates how consensus rules push climate ambition into voluntary side tracks with weaker enforcement.
insights.locator: However, this was still short of the 196 parties

insights.claim: By the end of COP30, 93 countries had signed on, committing to develop voluntary pathways to reverse forest loss and degradation by 2030.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Broad but voluntary buy-in sets the baseline for forest-policy and finance announcements at COP31.
insights.locator: By the end of the summit, 93 countries

insights.claim: The roadmap sits in a line of forest pledges: 2014 New York Declaration (39 countries), 2021 Glasgow Leaders' Declaration (140+ countries), and the 2023 COP28 global stocktake, where halting deforestation by 2030 was first in negotiated text.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
entities: Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration on Forests and Land Use
insights.so_what: Repeated 2030 pledges without delivery raise execution risk on the 2030 target.
insights.locator: The deforestation roadmap is the latest

insights.claim: The roadmap aims to 'translate forest-related outcomes into coordinated, country-led action' rather than win new signatories, because COP28 and the Kunming-Montreal framework already contain consensus commitments.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Reframes success as implementation, not signature counts.
insights.quote: So we don’t need any country to subscribe to the roadmap.

insights.claim: The roadmap has three pillars (national action, international action, financial mechanisms), each with current actions, enabling conditions and COP30 presidency proposals.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A modular menu lets countries pick policies, so uptake will be uneven.

insights.claim: For national action the roadmap lists 18 policy approaches across five forest dimensions (maintain, sustainable use, degradation, deforestation, restoration), including protected areas, Indigenous territorial rights, and restricting permits for forest conversion, and proposes a five-step process.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Policy menu points to where public funding and regulatory activity are likely to go.

insights.claim: On trade, the roadmap says measures that reward compliance are generally more effective than those imposing additional economic and administrative burdens on exporters, and it prioritises deforestation-free trade policies.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Favours incentive-based over penalty-based trade rules, relevant to exporters of forest-risk commodities.

insights.claim: The roadmap estimates countries need about $300bn per year by 2030 to halt and reverse deforestation, but current finance is under one-third of that, with nearly 90% from domestic public finance.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A roughly $200bn+ annual gap, mostly external, underpins demand for forest finance and carbon-market instruments.
insights.quote: The roadmap notes that countries need an estimated $300bn per year by 2030 to halt and reverse deforestation, yet current finance reaches less than one-third of that figure.

insights.claim: The roadmap makes 10 forest-finance proposals, including aligning domestic finance flows, benefit-sharing measures, and strengthening forests' position in carbon markets.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Carbon-market integration is a named lever for closing the forest funding gap.

insights.claim: Brazil's deforestation rate has fallen to its lowest level on record, down more than 70% since 2022, according to Corrêa do Lago.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Brazil is using its domestic record as proof of concept, which supports its credibility on forest finance such as the Tropical Forest Forever Facility.

insights.claim: Roadmap monitoring needs are uneven: countries' capacity to access and use forest-monitoring information 'remains uneven', with calls for technical cooperation and capacity-building.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Satellite and fire-monitoring support is a recurring demand from countries.
insights.locator: The roadmap highlights some of the global forest-monitoring

insights.claim: India historically opposes top-down mitigation and land-use commitments and objected to linking trade with forests; at COP30 it objected to voluntary roadmaps outside the COP agenda, yet its environment minister later said India 'welcomes' the forest roadmap and endorses the Tropical Forest Forever Facility.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: India's softened tone suggests political resistance may be procedural more than substantive.

insights.claim: Russia opposes a universal roadmap, arguing such initiatives are not mandated under the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement architecture, and also objects on trade grounds; it notes no legally binding definition of forest degradation while calling wildfires a key driver.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Russia's boreal forest and definitional objections point to enduring friction on land-use rules.
insights.quote: does not support the development of a universal roadmap

insights.claim: Some countries were wary of non-negotiated mitigation commitments outside the COP agenda crowding out other items such as adaptation finance.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Agenda trade-offs between mitigation side tracks and adaptation finance may shape COP31 dynamics.

insights.claim: Corrêa do Lago said 'The climate change agenda is advancing faster than the negotiations [themselves], so we restructured the agenda.'
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals a shift toward coalitions of the willing outside formal UN consensus.
insights.quote: The climate change agenda is advancing faster than the negotiations [themselves], so we restructured the agenda.

insights.claim: Countries' submissions cited overlapping barriers: extractive pressure (Guyana, Suriname), agricultural expansion (EU, Switzerland, Mexico), illegal loggers outbidding conservation (Norway, Mexico), inconsistent definitions of degradation (Canada, Russia), and firewood reliance (Sudan, 70% of population).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Standing forests are undervalued against extraction, so payment-for-conservation schemes need to out-compete commodity returns.

insights.claim: Forest-rich countries want predictable, affordable climate finance, and the Coalition for Rainforest Nations asked for a clear assessment of total funding needed, while donors emphasise domestic, private and innovative finance (UK blended finance, Australia biodiversity credits, Norway repurposing harmful subsidies).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A donor-recipient split between public grants and private/market finance defines forest finance prospects.

insights.claim: Intensifying wildfires are a threat cited by Canada, Indonesia, Russia, Azerbaijan and Australia, and AOSIS wants mangroves included in forest definitions, noting climate impacts already degrade them.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Fire detection and monitoring are emerging demand areas for technical support.
